title: Technical deep dive: Autoscaling & capacity planning
summary: Deep dive on autoscaling and capacity planning for Catalyst Retail's LLM inference workload. Discussed burst policies, reserved GPUs vs. shared capacity, queueing models, latency SLOs, KV cache warmup, batching strategies, quantization tradeoffs, and VPC/on-prem constraints. Agreed next steps: Redwood to share capacity model, sample cost comparison, and run a 2-week pilot to collect perf metrics behind their VPC.
next_steps: Jordan to send capacity planning spreadsheet and cost model by 2026-05-22
Priya to schedule a pilot run window with Samir for last week of May
Customer to share sample production traces and percentiles (p50/p95/p99) by 2026-05-25
Agree on pilot success criteria (p95 < 250ms for chat, cost per 1k tokens target)
action_items: Jordan: send capacity model and reserved GPU pricing - due 2026-05-22
Priya: provide pilot run checklist and config template - due 2026-05-21

transcript:
Meeting header: Date: 2026-05-20 Start: 16:00 UTC Duration: ~52 minutes Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (Catalyst CTO), Rafael Torres (Head of ML), Samir Iqbal (Infra) [00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Um, we're gonna run through autoscaling and capacity planning for your inference fleet. Really excited to dig in. Quick roll call? [00:12] Maya Chen: Hi Maya here. [00:14] Rafael Torres: Rafael, hey. [00:16] Samir Iqbal: Samir, yep. [00:18] Jordan Lee: Great. Priya, do you want to intro? [00:21] Priya Desai: Sure, I'm Priya, I work on runtime perf and infra. We'll focus on tradeoffs between reserved GPUs and shared hosted, burst policies, queueing, kv cache behavior and batching. We'll also cover quantization impacts and VPC considerations. [00:36] Maya Chen: Cool. Our context: we run product recs and chat assistant, peak traffic during promotions. Latency SLOs are tight for chat - p95 under 250ms ideally, cost pressure on batch recs. We're evaluating Redwood Dedicated vs Hosted for initial rollout behind our VPC. [00:54] Jordan Lee: Makes sense. Rafael, what are your current model sizes and request patterns? [00:58] Rafael Torres: Mostly a 7B conversation model for chat, and a 13B for reranking and recs. Chat is lower tokens per request but needs low tail latency; recs are higher throughput tolerant of slightly higher latency. Traffic pattern is spikey - 10x from baseline during flash sales, bursts last 20-40 minutes. [01:20] Priya Desai: Ok that spike profile is useful. Two main knobs: reserved capacity (Dedicated) to guarantee baseline throughput and a burst policy to absorb short spikes. We also support queueing with backpressure and graceful degradation to lighter quantized variants. [01:40] Samir Iqbal: Quick question — how does the kv cache warmup affect tail latency when you spin up new replicas? We had issues where chat latencies spiked when new pods started because the cache was cold. [01:52] Priya Desai: Great question. With our runtime the KV cache is per-replica KV for attention states; warmup is a function of request diversity. Strategies: keep a small pool of hot workers with warmed caches (reserved), or use proactive pre-warming by replaying representative prompts at scale on new nodes. We typically recommend maintaining a small stand-by pool for chat SLOs. [02:18] Rafael Torres: So is that a fixed number of GPUs or per-model? What about cost? [02:23] Jordan Lee: You can reserve a base number of GPU slots per model family; reserved pricing is discounted versus on-demand. Then burst capacity can be configured to draw from shared capacity or burst to compatible smaller quantized variants. We'll send you the pricing sheet. [02:36] Maya Chen: Can you explain how the queueing model works? We don't want long queues to break UX, but we can accept some retries. [02:43] Priya Desai: We support two queueing policies: short-latency-first (reject or requeue after short timeout) and batch-first (favor throughput). For chat we suggest latency-first with a short admission timeout (e.g., 200ms) and an autopromote to a smaller quantized model if queue exceeds threshold. There's also adaptive batching: small requests are coalesced up to a target batch size depending on measured latency. [03:11] Jordan Lee: Practically, that means during a spike we'll keep the p95 stable by refusing excess requests fast or sending them to a cheaper quantized model. That helps maintain UX for the accepted requests. [03:25] Samir Iqbal: What's the overhead of switching to quantized variants? Any quality regression? Rafael: We tested 4-bit on a subset and saw a small drop in perplexity but acceptable for recs, not for critical safety flows. [03:40] Priya Desai: Right, quantization is workload-dependent. Our recommendations: use int8/4 quant for background reranks, but reserve FP16 or higher for chat passages where hallucination risk is higher. Also, quantized variants are often faster and allow higher burst concurrency on the same physical GPU. [03:59] Maya Chen: For warm-up, is the kv cache persisted across restarts? [04:03] Priya Desai: Not persisted across process restarts. It's in-memory keyed by session prompt prefix. So if a worker restarts you lose that warmed KV and see higher first-request latency. That's why a reserved hot pool helps.
[04:16] Rafael Torres: Could you do some kind of persistent cache layer at network level? Like an external KV? [04:21] Priya Desai: We don't persist KV cache externally because the cache needs to be tightly coupled to the runtime for speed; network hops add latency. Instead the pattern is sticky routing to warm nodes or proactive warmers in the same node group. [04:35] Jordan Lee: On autoscaling, our system supports reactive scale based on queue depth and latency SLOs, plus scheduled scaling for predictable events. The scaling latency depends on GPU spin-up time — for Dedicated it's faster since machines are pre-provisioned; for Hosted bursting to shared GPUs there can be some provisioning delay. [04:55] Samir Iqbal: What's typical spin-up time? [04:58] Priya Desai: For Dedicated pre-warmed nodes, essentially negligible (seconds) because capacity is already there; adding more VMs to a pool might be 2-8 minutes depending on provider. For hosted cold capacity it's variable, often 5-15 minutes. So you should avoid relying on cold provisioning for minute-level spikes. [05:18] Rafael Torres: Our spikes are 20-40 minutes — could be okay to rely on hosted burst if we can accept a few minutes of degraded perf? [05:25] Jordan Lee: Possibly, but better approach: reserve enough baseline to cover most of steady-state plus short bursts, and use hosted burst only for extreme events. Also configure two tiers: warm standby nodes and a larger cold pool that can be spun up if needed. [05:39] Maya Chen: How do you recommend we size baseline? We have historical traces — how do you translate that into GPU counts? [05:47] Priya Desai: We'll take your p50/p95/p99 latency and request qps histograms. Our model uses per-token throughput per GPU for the given model/quantization and average tokens per request to compute concurrent slots. We can run a capacity plan spreadsheet to show reserve vs burst scenarios. Jordan will send the template. [06:06] Rafael Torres: What's the math for queueing? Do you model an M/M/c queue or something else? [06:11] Priya Desai: Good ears. We use a hybrid model — an M/G/c approximation with empirical service-time distributions from our runtimes. We simulate queue depth and latency under the arrival histogram and include startup/warmup delays. That gives a more realistic tail compared to pure M/M/c assumptions. [06:30] Samir Iqbal: Are there autoscaler policies to prefer spinning up nodes in the same AZ for latency / data locality, especially in our VPC? [06:38] Jordan Lee: Yes, you can constrain scaling to specific AZs or regions. For Private deployments you control placement entirely. For Hosted we try to route to same region to minimize cross-AZ latency, but reserved Dedicated pools are best for locality guarantees. [06:51] Maya Chen: Security - if we do VPC peering, how does Redwood access the cluster? We need to ensure no traffic leaves our network. [06:59] Jordan Lee: For Redwood Private we offer a customer-managed control plane and optional on-prem package; for VPC peering we use private links and the data path can stay within your network. We'll share our network diagram and SOC2 artifacts. [07:12] Rafael Torres: Any thoughts on multi-tenant GPU utilization? We want to pack many small requests to keep GPU utilization high but avoid noisy neighbor latency spikes. [07:21] Priya Desai: Continuous batching and request shaping helps — we dynamically batch by latency budget and use QoS classes to isolate latency-sensitive traffic. For strict SLOs you reserve capacity; for cost-sensitive workloads we pack aggressively with per-request priority and preemption. [07:38] Rafael Torres: Ok. Can the runtime preempt lower-priority batches mid-generation? [07:42] Priya Desai: Not mid-token. We prefer admission control at request start. If a high-priority request arrives, it either goes to hot pool or we reject/requeue lower priority ones. There's no safe mid-stream preemption currently. [07:55] Jordan Lee: Let's talk concrete numbers — for your 7B chat model, on an A100-equivalent GPU in FP16 we can do roughly X tokens/sec (we'll put precise numbers in the spreadsheet). Quantized int8/4 variants can increase concurrency by ~1.5-2x but with quality tradeoffs. [08:13] Maya Chen: We'll need those numbers per model and quantization. Also, show cost per 1k tokens with reserved vs hosted. [08:19] Jordan Lee: Totally. We'll produce a cost vs latency matrix. [08:23] Priya Desai: Also note cold-start KV warmup adds a penalty to the first few requests; in simulation we add a warmup penalty window dependent on session stickiness. If you have long-lived sessions we see much less tail variance. [08:38] Samir Iqbal: For the pilot, we want Redwood to run a load test inside our VPC — can you run head-to-head: reserved only, reserved + burst to hosted, and quantized fallback paths? [08:48] Jordan Lee: Yep, that's the typical pilot. We'll run three scenarios, collect p50/p95/p99, cost per token, and failure rates. Priya will own test config. [08:58] Rafael Torres: One more — how do we handle model rollouts and version pinning across pools? Like can we route traffic to older model variant in a canary while reserving majority to stable one? [09:06] Priya Desai: Yes — rollouts are per-route and per-model. You can do canary percentages, and we can pin canaries to specific pools to avoid noisy neighbor interference. [09:16] Jordan Lee: Time check — anyone want to dive deeper on math or should we move to next steps? [09:20] Maya Chen: Let's jump to next steps then follow up via the pilot. [09:24] Priya Desai: Ok last bits — we'll include recommended thresholds: standby pool for chat covering 30-50% of peak, admission timeout 150-250ms, auto-quantize threshold at queue > 2x baseline. Those are starting points, not hard rules. [09:39] Rafael Torres: Noted. Also Samir will share our network ACLs. [09:43] Samir Iqbal: Yep will do. [09:46] Jordan Lee: Recap: Jordan to send capacity spreadsheet and cost matrix; Priya to prepare pilot configs and warm-up scripts; Samir to share traces and network details; customer to confirm pilot window. [09:58] Maya Chen: Sounds good. Thanks everyone. [10:00] Rafael Torres: Thanks. [10:02] Priya Desai: Thanks all. Notes on transcription: Some words garbled (e.g., "Red wood" instead of Redwood), speaker labels occasionally simplified. Transcript captures technical details and next steps. Attachments referenced: capacity-planning-template.xlsx (link sent), SOC2-summary.pdf (link), pilot-config.yml (link)
